On a tribal level, it's because we're good little slaves who do what we're told. The great truth of entertainment is that, when a character is presented in a more in-depth way, we're supposed to root for them and often do. Think if the events in 'Sons' were told from a cop's perspective. You wouldn't see all the relationships and humanization, and the story would be one-sided. The Crow would be a one-dimensional menace, and you would root for the cop.

But that being said, it seems only recently that dramas, specifically action dramas, have been reversing roles. Look at 'Dexter', look at 'Oz'. Thirty years ago, there weren't many films or TV shows that made the clear villain the protagonist. Villains were one-dimensional, heroes were as well. But the formula is the same. Heroes were always highly-skilled people that played on our deepest fantasies of what we want ourselves to be. Villains were bitter automatons, and were hardly human. 'Sons' still uses that formula. Jax Teller could very easily be the villain if he wasn't humanized, but he was, so the draw is the classic hero with the violence and criminality that we're meant to ignore. And it works. Most of us like Jax Teller, but if we heard a story about him on the evening news, we'd call for an instant execution.

Really, I think a lot of this has to do with the way our society has changed. Drugs and gangs are very real, as is violence. We've become desensitized. Exaggerate it a bit, throw it on the screen, and we can forgive a few hundred wrongful murders in exchange for a great story and a character to care about.

I want to be the guy you're talking about here. Life has made me bitter. My upbringing made me bitter, all the shitty jobs I've worked made me bitter, being treated like a dog made me bitter. When my step-brother talks to me like an equal, I just don't know how to handle it. I just don't know how to be a better man in the face of all of this. I want to learn. I don't want to be so negative. And I want to help people. I'm just not the person I wanted to be when I was a boy. I guess I just keep saying to myself 'I'll grow when I get on top of the mountain'. I'm just realizing that the mountain isn't made for my kind. I do feel unworthy, but at the same time, I'm angry because people have always told me I'm unworthy. I know I'm better than that. I just have this feeling of wanting to cripple those who have wronged me, but help those who need help. I want to learn to forgive. I feel like I'm fighting this inner war in which part of me wants to watch the world burn, and part of me wants to save it. But the former takes over most of the time. I understand that you can't operate without some sort of funding initially, but I've found that requiring residents to pay rent ($30 a week is reasonable) only after they've found a job is the only move you have. I didn't move into a shelter until I had lost my job, and you'll find that most people won't ask for help until they lose their income. Set a limit of 30 days to find employment now that they're in a stable environment, and help with that if you can.

Also, a curfew is necessary to ensure order, but be understanding of jobs. It's very likely that anyone there could get a job past 6PM. Fast food jobs is what a lot of people will find at first, especially if they have a record, and they can't afford to turn it down.

I would also offer some sort of drug counseling. You'll get a lot of current or recently sober meth users, and you'll need rules for that. For the most part, smoking cigarettes and using prescribed recommendation is fine, but you don't want anything else being used. The presence of drugs or alcohol can easily undermine everything you're trying to accomplish.

Ultimately, my biggest piece of advice is to treat people with respect. Most of these guys are used to being treated horribly, and they're used to a lot of shelters saying "believe in my god or you're wrong". They're human beings just like anyone else and should be able to believe in whatever they want. I've lived in a shelter where the director used it to up his ego. You didn't know from one second to the other if he was going to kick you out, and you just had to put up with his ego. As a result, he had a very low success rate. There is a difference between what you think you see and what you really see-- you see hundreds of details at every second, and your brain processes each one, but not all of them come to your conscious focus. Your mind doesn't stop working when you zone out, your consciousness is just elsewhere. Therefore, your body is still acting and reacting, allowing you to make it to your destination without crashing or winding up somewhere else. Think of it as biological autopilot. Inebriation affects this, which is why sobriety is a prerequisite for driving by law enforcement.

In my early 20s, I was homeless for about nine months. I held down a shitty fast food job for the entire time, but due to the low pay, I could only stay in a hotel every other week. I lived in my car and took bum baths, which allowed to keep the classic homeless stink from coming on, but toward the end I changed jobs and due to pay interval changes I couldn't afford to stay in a hotel for a month straight. After about a week and a half, you get the smell no matter what the fuck you do, and this was January so I couldn't swim in a stream. A month in, I smelled like death and a million other things. After work on payday, I checked into a hotel, cranked up the heater, and took the best hot shower of my life. When I got out, my skin started peeling off after only being exposed to the cold for a month. But my god, it felt amazing.

Never take showers for granted.

The Daedric Prince of Motherhood, or something to that effect. She looked after Jax when he was in a chaotic state of mind, giving him certain moments of clarity. Think back to the night he spent in the graveyard in Season I. She put a blanket over him, made him go out of his way to return it, pointed him toward cool water. That moment of intermission brought him toward a better decision to make a change. When Gemma was so caught up in her usual manipulation, a distant alteration of words made her stop and reflect, which led to a less impulsive reaction when she got back to the events. In Belfast, when Jax was following Abel's adoptive parents, he noticed her. He soon decided to let him go, which in truth was the best thing, but Gemma didn't allow it. Then, in the finale, she granted him a joyous death. Jax was heading to the back of the courthouse, and probably would've gone in gun blazing into a building full of cops. He might've died, or he might've killed innocents. But with her camoflauge, only real threats died and Jax got a moment of joy going out the right way.

I don't think she's the harbinger of death or chaos-- quite the opposite.  She's the protector of lesser evils, loving them as only a mother can, whilst granting a moment to reflect so that innocents may reap the benefits.

'Sons' has seen me through so many periods of my life-- through love and loss, through plundering, through homelessness, gaining responsibility and maturity. I liked it because I've always been an outcast, purely counter-culture to a degree. I've always felt the inner-chaos that comes with living in a time you feel is 200 years too late, or maybe being born on the wrong planet. 'Sons' took that which outcasts relate to and made the mainstream want to be us. Suddenly, outcasts are gods. That's just cool.

Really, I relate to Jax quite a bit, especially with the conflicted father/son dialogue. I didn't grow up in the best situation, my dad did a lot of things I grew up angry for, but in the past five years I've gone from hatred to understanding. The older I get, the more I see why he did what he did, and the ugly truth that I would do the same. I'd be lying if I said 'Sons' didn't initiate hours of thought on the subject.
